<reason>CON ran a disciplined, narrow case: the motion is overbroad because it forbids one legitimate category (vetted planners analyzing precise trajectories in secure environments), while conceding all abusive sales should be banned regardless of consent. PRO immediately exploited that concession, shrinking the debate to a single sympathetic exception, then won the weighing on failure modes: a regulator misjudging a "commuter behavior" front produces an irreversible personal disclosure, whereas the motion's failure yields a thinner volunteer dataset. PRO's reframing of "excluded" as "asked" defused CON's selection-bias point, and its observation that transport planning is the use people would most plausibly consent to blunted the claimed loss. CON's strongest live point—that PRO still permits brokers to analyze nonconsenting traces for aggregates, so planner access adds only marginal risk—was met with the "second custodian" argument, which CON credibly contested, but CON's own admission that "no remedy can undo disclosure" was turned against it in PRO's closing. PRO did shift from "the motion doesn't cover this" to "yes it does, and that's fine," which CON correctly flagged, and PRO's opening was clipped; these cost it a little. Overall PRO made the decision cleaner and the stakes more concrete, and CON never showed why an extra consent gate in its own sealed room is unaffordable rather than merely inconvenient.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Rebuttal 1 [B2.1–B2.9]: seizing CON's concession that abusive sales must be banned regardless of consent, reducing the dispute to "one sympathetic transport planner," attacking purpose-licensing as adjudicating intentions before an unrecallable file leaves the building, and turning the selection-bias argument into a "captive population" that logically demands compulsory tracking. This set the frame CON spent the rest of the debate fighting inside.</best_rebuttal>
